chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Math of Portfolio Construction

lessons.title: Check Size, Ownership Targets, and Capital Allocation Across a Portfolio

body.text: Cheque size is not a feeling. It is the output of three decisions made in order: how much capital you have actually earmarked for initial bets, how many of those bets you need, and how much conviction any single deal has earned.

children.text: Chapter 1 left you with an initial-cheque budget carved out of your total corpus, after reserves, and a position-count target chosen to give the power law a real chance of showing up. The previous lesson showed that your expected multiple on any single deal is set by price relative to expected value. This lesson connects the two: how to turn a fixed pool of initial-cheque capital into an actual sizing plan across every position, without either spraying too thin to matter or concentrating so hard that a handful of bad calls sink the whole plan.
Two Ways to Size a Cheque: Fixed Amount vs. Ownership Target

There are two starting philosophies for sizing a cheque, and most working angel portfolios end up as some blend of the two. The first writes a fixed rupee amount into every deal, regardless of valuation, and lets ownership percentage float with whatever that round is priced at. The second sets a target ownership percentage first, and lets the cheque size float with the valuation, writing whatever amount is needed to hit that stake.

body.title: Fixed Cheque Size vs. Ownership Target

columns.label: Fixed Cheque Size
points: Capital deployment is fully predictable across the portfolio
Easy to plan position count against a fixed budget
Ownership floats, so you own less of expensive rounds and more of cheap ones, whether or not that matches your conviction

columns.label: Ownership Target
points: Keeps your stake, and therefore your dollar-for-dollar exposure to a winner, consistent across deals
Cheque size balloons as valuations rise, straining a fixed budget exactly in the priciest, most competitive rounds
Requires knowing the valuation before you can even size the cheque, which is not always available early in a process

body.caption: The ownership-target approach in one line. As post-money valuation rises, so does the cheque needed to hold your target stake.
Cheque required to hit a 1% ownership target, at different valuations

body.text: This is the tension a pure ownership-target strategy runs into fast. It forces you to write your biggest cheques into your most expensive rounds, exactly where the previous lesson showed expected multiple is already under the most pressure. Most working angels do not run a pure ownership-target strategy for this reason, they cap it with a maximum cheque per deal, effectively blending it with the fixed-amount approach.

children.text: The practical compromise most experienced angels settle into is a small number of fixed tiers, each with its own cheque size, reserved for a defined level of conviction. This keeps sizing decisions fast and consistent, while still letting your very best ideas get meaningfully larger cheques than your speculative ones. Picking up the ₹60 lakh initial-cheque budget from Chapter 1 (the 60% of a ₹1 crore corpus not held back as reserve), here is one way to structure it.

body.title: How the ₹60 Lakh Initial-Cheque Budget Splits Across Tiers

body.text: The tier a deal gets assigned to should be decided before you know how much you wish you could write, not after. It is tempting to promote a deal to High-Conviction retroactively just because a round is closing fast and excitement is high, which is precisely the FOMO dynamic Lesson 2.1 warned about. Decide the tier from your diligence, then let the tier decide the cheque, not the other way round.

body.title: Rebuild the Tiers for a Different Budget
body.prompt: You have ₹90,00,000 earmarked for initial cheques. You plan 12 Explore positions at ₹3,00,000 each and 6 Core positions at ₹5,00,000 each, and want to put whatever remains into a single High-Conviction cheque. How large can that High-Conviction cheque be? Answer in rupees, e.g. 500000.
body.explanation: Explore: 12 × ₹3,00,000 = ₹36,00,000. Core: 6 × ₹5,00,000 = ₹30,00,000. Together: ₹66,00,000. Remaining from ₹90,00,000: ₹24,00,000. That remainder is what the single High-Conviction cheque can be sized up to. Always add up every tier's total before sizing what is left, a rushed subtraction here is an easy real-world mistake with real money behind it.

children.text: The Ownership Floor: When a Cheque Is Too Small to Matter

There is a practical floor below which a cheque, however good the deal, stops being worth the effort. A ₹2 lakh Explore-tier cheque into a round priced at ₹30 crore post-money buys well under 0.1% ownership, a stake small enough that it may not clear the thresholds many term sheets use to define who gets pro-rata rights or regular information updates from the company. This is exactly why Indian angel syndication platforms exist, LetsVenture, Indian Angel Network, 100X.VC, and Titan Capital among others pool many individual angels' smaller cheques into a single line on the company's cap table, crossing that meaningful-ownership floor collectively even where any one angel's personal cheque could not have on its own. Chapter 5 covers syndicates and co-investing as a diversification tool in full.

body.text: Which rights attach to which ownership thresholds (pro-rata, information rights, board observer seats) varies deal by deal and is negotiated into each term sheet, not a fixed rule across the market. Read the actual term sheet for any deal rather than assuming a stake above or below some round number automatically comes with or without these rights.

body.title: Check Against Your Own Ownership Floor
body.prompt: You have set yourself a personal ownership floor of 0.75%, below which you skip a deal regardless of how much you like it. A round is being raised at ₹22 crore post-money. What is the minimum cheque required to hit your 0.75% floor? Answer in ₹ lakh, e.g. 10 for ₹10,00,000.
body.explanation: 0.75% × ₹22 crore = ₹16,50,000, or ₹16.5 lakh. If your tier structure caps this deal's cheque below ₹16.5 lakh, either the deal does not clear your ownership floor at this valuation, or you need a route, like a syndicate, that lets your capital combine with others to reach it.

body.title: A Great Deal, Priced Above Your Floor
body.scenario: You have done real diligence on a startup and it clearly belongs in your High-Conviction tier. The round, however, is pricing at a valuation where your usual ₹8 lakh High-Conviction cheque would only buy an ownership stake well below the 0.75% floor you set for yourself.
body.prompt: What are your realistic options here, and which would you lean towards?
body.modelAnswer: There are broadly three options. First, write a larger cheque than your usual tier to hit the floor, which means pulling capital from elsewhere in your plan, ideally from the reserve or from a lower-conviction Explore allocation rather than breaking your total budget. Second, invest through a syndicate or co-investment vehicle that pools your cheque with others to collectively clear a meaningful ownership line on the cap table, even if your individual cheque alone would not. Third, accept the smaller stake and invest anyway, treating this specific position as a deliberate exception to the floor rather than pretending the floor does not apply. What you should not do is quietly lower your floor for this one deal because you are excited about it and never revisit that lowered bar again, that is how ownership-floor discipline erodes deal by deal until it stops meaning anything.

points: Fixed cheque sizing keeps deployment predictable but lets ownership float with valuation; ownership-target sizing keeps stakes consistent but lets cheque size balloon in expensive rounds
A conviction-tiered structure, a small number of fixed cheque sizes matched to diligence-based conviction levels, is the practical middle ground most angels actually use
Assign the tier from your diligence before you know deal momentum, not after, or FOMO will quietly promote deals that do not deserve it

There is a practical ownership floor below which a cheque may not carry meaningful rights or influence, and Indian syndication platforms exist specifically to help individual angels clear that floor collectively
Every sizing decision should be checked against the initial-cheque budget that remains after the reserve carve-out from Chapter 1, not against total corpus
